title: Counting beats
teaches: Two oscillators: beating, detune, thickness, and the intervals of music

blocks.text: **The sound.** One oscillator sounds like one thin instrument. The string pads of 1970s records and the huge leads of 1990s dance music sound like a whole section playing at once. Here is the thin version and the big one.

blocks.caption: One saw, and a sound like a section of them

blocks.text: The secret is in a sound piano tuners spend their lives trying to get rid of. Most notes on a piano have two or three strings each, struck together by one hammer. A piano tuner has to get each set exactly in tune with itself. Strange to say, they don't do it by judging the pitch. They listen for something else: a slow swelling and fading in the sound, a wah-wah-wah, which tells them the strings are slightly apart. They turn the tuning pin until it slows, and slows, and stops.

blocks.caption: Two pure tones, the first at 440 Hz and the second slightly above it, and the sum the ear hears over one second.
blocks.task: Guess, then tune the second tone until the beating stops

blocks.text: These are **[[beats]]**. Two tones a few hertz apart drift in and out of step. When their peaks line up they add and the sound swells; half a cycle later (half of one wave's rise and fall) one pushes while the other pulls, they cancel, and it fades. The number of swells a second is simply the difference between the two frequencies: 440 and 443 beat three times a second. It is the most precise tool a tuner has, sensitive to a fraction of a hertz.
A synth with two oscillators can do the same on purpose. The second plays the same wave as the first, and its **Level** sets how much of it you hear.

blocks.caption: The synth with a second oscillator, so far switched off.
blocks.task: Bring Level up to 55 % or more

blocks.text: Exactly in tune, two identical oscillators are simply one oscillator, louder. Everything interesting happens when they are not.

**Detune** pulls the second oscillator slightly off pitch, measured in **cents**, hundredths of a semitone.[^cents] The two drift in and out of step, and you hear the beating as a slow swell. More detune beats faster; so do higher notes, because the same number of cents is more hertz higher up.

blocks.caption: Both oscillators on, with the second's detune.
blocks.task: Hear it with no detune at all, and at 40 cents

blocks.text: A slight detune makes a sound thicker, the way a section of twelve violins sounds bigger than one violin played louder: no two players are ever quite in tune, and their beating smears into a rich, moving sound called a chorus. Synth designers took the idea as far as it goes in the late 1990s with the **supersaw**, seven saw waves detuned around one note, which became the sound of trance music.[^supersaw]

Move the second oscillator further, by a whole musical interval, and it stops thickening the note and starts making a chord. **Interval** sets it an octave down, in unison, a fifth up or an octave up. An octave is a frequency twice as high. A fifth is one and a half times as high, the ratio 3 to 2, the jump from the first “twinkle” to the second in “Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star”.

These ratios sound smooth together because of their harmonics. A note on 200 Hz has harmonics at 200, 400, 600, 800. A fifth above, 300 Hz, has 300, 600, 900, 1200. They share 600 and 1200, so those harmonics don't beat. Tune the fifth slightly off and the shared harmonics split and beat, and the chord sounds sour. On a piano, tuned in [[equal temperament]], every fifth is left a shade narrow on purpose and beats slowly. This is how tuners set fifths, and it is the start of an answer to why some notes sound good together, which a later lesson takes up.[^fifths]

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Two tones a few hertz apart beat at the difference between them.
Slight detune thickens a sound; a whole interval makes a chord.
Simple ratios (2:1, 3:2) share harmonics, which is why they sound smooth.

blocks.text: With Level at Off there is only one oscillator, so Detune and Interval go dark. And in unison with no detune the two are the same tone, only louder. Then Level itself goes dark: you can't tell how loud the second oscillator is when it is indistinguishable from the first.

blocks.caption: Level, Detune and Interval together.
blocks.task: Turn Level dark without touching it: use Interval and Detune

blocks.text: Back to the big sound from the start. Its pitch is the same as the thin saw's, so it is one note made thick rather than a chord, and the second oscillator is in unison. How fast it swells or shimmers sets the detune, and how strongly the beats dip sets the balance between the two oscillators: the swells fade all the way to silence only when both are equally loud.

blocks.caption: Both oscillators, the second starting a fifth up and switched off. Find the section's settings.
blocks.task: Make the thin saw into the section

blocks.text: String machines of the 1970s, like the ARP Solina,[^solina] did this with a chorus circuit that copied the sound and wobbled the copy's pitch, so the beating never settled. The supersaw does it with seven oscillators. The idea is the same as the tuner's beats, used the other way: not to find where two strings agree, but to keep them from ever agreeing.

blocks.caption: Six questions on two oscillators
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Two tones at 440 Hz and 444 Hz play together. How many times a second does the sound swell?
items.why: The beat rate is the difference between the frequencies: 444 - 440 = 4.

items.ask: A tuner hears the beating between two strings slow down. What is happening?
choices: The strings are getting closer in pitch
The strings are getting further apart
The hammer is hitting more softly
items.why: Fewer beats a second means a smaller difference in frequency.

items.ask: Why does detuning a second oscillator slightly make a sound thicker?
choices: The two drift in and out of step, like players never quite in tune
items.why: The slow beating between nearly equal tones gives the moving, chorused sound of a section.

items.ask: A note is at 200 Hz. What is a fifth above it?
items.why: A fifth is the ratio 3:2: 200 × 1.5 = 300 Hz.

items.ask: Why do an octave and a fifth sound smooth?
choices: Their harmonics coincide, so they don't beat
items.why: Simple ratios put many harmonics of the two notes on the same frequencies.

items.ask: Why does Level go dark when the second oscillator is in unison with no detune?
choices: It is then the same tone as the first, just louder
items.why: Identical oscillators can't be told apart, so their balance can't be heard.

summary: **Two tones a few hertz apart beat**: the sound swells and fades at the difference between them.
**Piano tuners listen for beats**, and turn the pin until they stop.
**A second oscillator, slightly detuned, thickens a sound** like a section of players never quite in tune.
**Detune is measured in cents**, hundredths of a semitone.
**Whole intervals make chords**: an octave is 2:1, a fifth 3:2.
**Simple ratios share harmonics**, so they don't beat; slightly off, they do.

supersaw.title: The supersaw
supersaw.text: Roland's JP-8000 of 1996 offered a waveform it called the super saw: seven saws spread around the note with a single knob for how far apart. It was copied by nearly every synth that followed. Its tone is a mass of slow, overlapping beats that never repeat, which is why it sounds huge.

fifths.title: Tuning a fifth by its beats
fifths.text: On a modern piano the fifths are deliberately a shade narrow, 700 cents instead of the pure 702, so that twelve fifths close up into seven octaves (equal temperament). A4 to E5 above it then beat about one and a half times a second: the third harmonic of A4 (1320 Hz) against the second of E5 (1318.5 Hz). Tuners set each fifth by counting that slow beat.

cents.title: Why cents and not hertz?
cents.text: An octave is always a doubling of frequency, whether from 110 to 220 Hz or from 440 to 880 Hz. Because the ear hears pitch in ratios, musicians divide every octave into 1200 equal steps called cents, 100 to each semitone. Ten cents of detune sounds the same amount sharp anywhere on the keyboard, even though it is under 0.2 Hz near the bottom of a piano and about 24 Hz near the top.

solina.title: The Solina String Ensemble
solina.text: The Solina was built in the Netherlands in 1974 by Eminent, a maker of home organs, and sold in America by ARP. Inside, a single oscillator bank drove all the keys at once (as in an organ), and a three-line bucket-brigade delay wobbled the pitch in three phases at once to mimic a string section. You can hear it on records by Pink Floyd, Herbie Hancock, Elton John and Air.
